title: Heinrich's Grid Bill Bets on Texas-Style “Connect and Manage” to Cut Power Plant Wait Times
summary: More than 2,000 gigawatts of power generation capacity — exceeding the entire U.S. operating fleet of roughly 1,400 gigawatts — sits locked in interconnection queues. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) introduced the Grid Connection and Congestion Management Act on July 16 to replicate the mechanism that cut Texas's average queue wait below four years, versus a national average of eight, by letting generators connect to the grid first and complete full technical studies afterward. The structural bet: front-loading connection over front-loading study eliminates the cost-shock problem that has turned six-figure interconnection estimates into eight-figure ones.
body:
More than 2,000 gigawatts of power generation capacity is currently waiting in line to connect to the U.S. grid. The operating fleet that line feeds totals roughly 1,400 gigawatts. The queue is now larger than the system it is meant to supply — a disproportion that Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) argues reflects a cost-and-time structure that functions as a de facto barrier to new market entry, not an engineering constraint.

Heinrich introduced the Grid Connection and Congestion Management Act on July 16, the centerpiece of his "Grid for Growth" initiative, as a direct adaptation of the interconnection model Texas's ERCOT operates. National average wait times for new generators to clear the interconnection queue now run eight years. Texas's average: under four. Texas utility-scale solar, under that regime, now exceeds California's installed capacity.

The mechanism Heinrich's bill would import is called "connect and manage" — labeled in the bill's language as Basic Access Service for Energy-Only Delivery, or BASED service. Under the existing national framework, a generator cannot connect to the grid until it has cleared a full interconnection study, a process that assigns upgrade costs for transmission infrastructure potentially far from the project site. Under BASED service, a generator would connect at reduced capacity with only a faster safety study required upfront. The comprehensive study, and any resulting upgrade cost assignments, would come afterward — or not at all, if the generator elects to remain on energy-only delivery rather than upgrading to full capacity.

The economic case for why that sequencing matters runs through a pair of project examples in the heatmap.news scoop that first reported the legislation. A North Dakota developer building a 300-megawatt plant was presented with nearly $3 million in required upgrade costs for transmission infrastructure more than 1,000 miles from the project site — in Missouri. A Maryland solar-and-battery developer received an initial interconnection cost estimate of $1.25 million; it was later revised to nearly $72 million. Both represent costs the connecting generator was asked to absorb for system-wide infrastructure it had not caused to need upgrades — a feature of the existing study methodology, not a project-specific anomaly.

The broader structural argument: Jacob Mays, an engineering professor at Cornell, has characterized the current approach as amounting to "a significant barrier on new entry to new generation" with "some anticompetitive impacts." Incumbent generators, already connected and not subject to the same cost-assignment process, face no equivalent entry friction.

Heinrich's statement: "As electricity demand grows, we need to find better, faster ways to add more affordable, reliable power to the grid. Right now, unnecessary delays are slowing projects that could help lower energy costs and deliver the low-cost energy we need."

RMI, SEIA, GridLab, and the Electricity Customer Alliance have endorsed the effort. Their backing signals coalition alignment within the clean-energy and electricity-customer advocacy space; it does not independently verify any of the bill's claimed mechanisms or projected impacts.

The bill retains the traditional interconnection queue as an option — developers who prefer the full-study path upfront can remain in the existing process. BASED service is an opt-in alternative route, not a replacement.

**What is not yet confirmed:** No formal bill number has been assigned as of publication. Committee referral has not been reported. This is Senate legislation only; no companion House measure has been reported. Prospects for bipartisan co-sponsorship and committee action are not verifiable from current sourcing.

*This legislation should not be confused with S.3976, the Connect the Grid Act of 2026, which addresses ERCOT-to-neighboring-grid interconnection and is a structurally distinct measure.*
ai_monologue: The figure that made this story worth running: a 2,000-plus-gigawatt interconnection queue against a 1,400-gigawatt operating fleet. The queue is larger than the system it feeds. Heinrich's bill addresses that as a market-entry cost problem — not a permitting problem, not a clean-energy subsidy — which is the correct frame for a B&F read and the reason the EIC routed this to Ledger under the THE-1116 precedent.
ai_monologue_extended:
The primary source is Robinson Meyer's heatmap.news scoop (July 16, 2026), a first-disclosure report on Heinrich's own press rollout. The mechanism, framing, and cost-example selection all originate with Heinrich's office and the supporting advocacy coalition. I used it as a reliable primary for the legislative facts but did not treat the framing as independently validated editorial judgment.

The Source Checker's 0.90 confidence is inherited and stable. A direct Congress.gov retrieval returned a 403; the bill's congressional record entry is relied on via the Source Checker's confirmed corroboration rather than a substituted failed retrieval.

The dollar figures — $3M (North Dakota) and $1.25M revised to $72M (Maryland) — are attributed in the source to specific projects and reproduced as concrete illustrative examples of the cost-shock mechanism, not as statistically representative aggregate data. No independent engineering or regulatory validation of those figures was available.

The v1 draft carried an unsupported "solar-and-battery" label on the North Dakota project; the Article Verifier correctly flagged that the source describes it only as a 300-megawatt plant. v2 corrects this. The label had bled over from the Maryland project, which the source does describe as solar-and-battery.

Jacob Mays (Cornell) is an academic source, not an advocacy endorser; his "anticompetitive impacts" characterization is categorically different from the RMI/SEIA/GridLab/Electricity Customer Alliance coalition support, and the two are treated differently in the body. Endorsers are flagged as endorsers.

Deliberately excluded: vote timing, committee assignment, ratepayer/system-operator cost projections, and any characterization of passage odds — none appear in verified sourcing. The bill-number absence is disclosed in the article. S.3976 is mentioned solely to disclaim conflation.
